newsitem.title: USA: IMF says will look at Ugandan military spending.
newsitem.headline: IMF says will look at Ugandan military spending.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund will look closely at Uganda's military spending in talks due this summer on an IMF-backed economic reform program, an IMF official said on Sunday.

"I am sure the budgetary burden of military spending on Uganda will be a subject in the forthcoming negotiations," Jack Boorman, director of the IMF's policy development and review department told a news conference.
The IMF is due to negotiate the renewal of a three-year program of economic reforms with Uganda this summer.
An IMF-approved program opens the way to debt reduction, and can encourage investment and aid flows by underpinning international confidence.

Boorman said Uganda had completed the easier "first generation" of economic reforms under a previous three-year plan, opening up its economy, and now faced the tougher task of implementing further free market reforms, like privatization.

Its track record on economic reforms so far, however, has already allowed it to become the first to benefit from a new debt relief initiative launched by the World Bank, IMF and Paris Club of official creditors to help poor countries.
That debt relief is due to start in April next year and will reduce Uganda's debt burden by about a fifth.
Boorman said the IMF would also look at providing transitional help to Uganda, but gave no details.
The World Bank has already pledged $75 million in grants in the interim period.
A number of countries, notably Germany, had expressed concern about the high proportion of Uganda's budget that goes to military spending.

World Bank head James Wolfensohn said on Friday, however, that he had received assurances from Ugandan President Yoweri Musseveni that money received from the debt relief -- meant for schools, hospitals and other social programs -- would not be diverted for arms spending.
